A recent Indian-parent Reddit discussion provides **anecdotal—not representative—evidence** that parents often:

- Begin childproofing when crawling or increased mobility starts.
- Piece together corner tabs, edge tape, locks, socket plugs and door guards from marketplaces.
- Find whole-home childproofing difficult because of limited space, cost or effort.
- Prefer protecting a room initially, but playpens can become impractical as children grow or resist confinement.
- Mention finger-pinching doors, sharp furniture, sockets and accessible cabinets as recognizable concerns. ([reddit.com](https://www.reddit.com/r/twoxindiamums/comments/1rw4o85/baby_proofing_recommendations/))

Authoritative guidance supports framing childproofing as helping children explore in a safer environment rather than promising an injury-proof home. UNICEF recommends inspecting each room from the child’s level, managing reachable hazards and not relying on supervision alone; it specifically mentions sharp furniture edges, sockets and locked storage for medicines and cleaning products. ([unicef.org](https://www.unicef.org/parenting/safety/how-to-babyproof-your-home?utm_source=openai))

   Show an ordinary Indian living room from a toddler’s low viewpoint, rapidly identifying six reachable zones before revealing the organized kit. This converts UNICEF’s child-level inspection advice into a strong visual device without using an accident reenactment.

2. **“Six marketplace searches versus one bucket”**  
   Split-screen execution: scattered tabs, multiple deliveries and installation confusion versus one labeled kit containing all six product categories. This directly dramatizes the brand’s most defensible convenience proposition and reflects the marketplace-sourcing behavior described by Indian parents. ([thepeachbucket.com](https://thepeachbucket.com/products/the-peach-bucket-6-in-1-child-safety-kit))

3. **“Let them explore; change the room”**  
   Begin with a parent repeatedly saying “No, don’t touch,” then transition to guards and locks installed around common Indian-home fixtures. Lead with reduced mental load and freer exploration—not “complete safety.” UNICEF similarly frames babyproofing as supporting exploration while managing hazards. ([unicef.org](https://www.unicef.org/parenting/safety/how-to-babyproof-your-home?utm_source=openai))

### Claim and execution cautions

- Prefer **“helps protect,” “reduces easy access,” “cushions”** and “covers six common danger zones.” Avoid “prevents injuries,” “100% safe,” “childproofs your entire home,” or implying supervision is unnecessary.
- Demonstrate only compatible fixtures actually tested by the brand; socket, adhesive and cabinet compatibility may vary.
- Claims including “food grade,” “BPA free,” “manually human tested,” “Made in India,” ₹20 lakh contributed, setup time and guarantees require internal substantiation before appearing prominently in paid ads. ([thepeachbucket.com](https://thepeachbucket.com/products/the-peach-bucket-6-in-1-child-safety-kit))
- Avoid graphic accidents or parental guilt. A curiosity-versus-environment framing is more credible and reusable.

### Access gaps and exact uncertainties

No access was available to verified buyer reviews, return reasons, support transcripts, creative history, ad-platform results, audience demographics, certification/test reports, actual inventory, product failure rates or installation-time measurements. It is therefore unknown which hazard or benefit converts best, whether ₹3,299 is price-competitive, and whether the public guarantees or safety/material claims are adequately documented."}

  "answer_markdown": "## Three ads to make this week

Your cheapest-click campaigns did **not** produce the best buyers: the Low CPM campaign generated ₹3.44 landing-page views but only 2 reported purchases at ₹2,532 each. Meanwhile, the Shopify broad campaign had expensive ₹33.92 landing-page views but delivered 24 purchases at ₹1,693 each. So these ads should **qualify parents**, not chase clicks: show the real kit, Indian-home use cases and ₹3,299 price early.

### 1) Reel: “Do the crawling-level check”
**Purpose:** Make six hazards instantly recognizable.

**Format:** 20–25 sec, 9:16. Film from toddler height in a real Indian home.

**Storyboard / on-screen copy:**
1. Camera crawls into living room: **“Your home looks different from down here.”**
2. Quick close-ups with labels: **Sharp edge · Corner · Socket · Cabinet · Fridge · Door**
3. Bucket lands in frame: **“6 common danger zones. 1 organised kit.”**
4. Rapid installation montage on compatible fixtures.
5. Final frame: **“The Peach Bucket 6-in-1 Child Safety Kit — ₹3,299”**
6. CTA: **“Check what’s inside”**

**Primary text:**
> When crawling begins, suddenly everything is within reach. The Peach Bucket brings six everyday childproofing essentials together for common furniture, sockets, cabinets, appliances and doors. One organised kit for ₹3,299. Adult supervision is still essential.

**Headline:** `See your home from their level`

**Designer note:** Avoid accident reenactments, red danger graphics and “complete protection.” Show only fixture types you have tested.

---

### 2) Carousel: “Six searches or one bucket?”
**Purpose:** Sell convenience while filtering for purchase intent.

**Format:** 7-card 4:5 carousel using clean product photography.

**Cards:**
1. **“Babyproofing your home shouldn’t take six separate searches.”**
2. **“8 m edge protection + 12 corner guards”**
3. **“12 socket guards”**
4. **“10 cabinet locks”**
5. **“2 fridge/microwave locks”**
6. **“4 door guards”**
7. **“All six categories in one organised kit — ₹3,299”**  
   CTA: **“Explore the kit”**

**Primary text:**
> Corner tabs from one seller. Socket guards from another. Cabinet locks from somewhere else—or one organised bucket containing six childproofing categories for common Indian-home danger zones. See everything included before you order.

**Headline:** `One kit instead of six searches`

**Designer note:** Put ₹3,299 on card 1 or 2 as well as the final card. This may reduce casual clicks, but should better qualify visitors. Don’t show marketplace logos or invent competitor prices.

---

### 3) UGC-style Reel: “I was tired of saying ‘don’t touch’”
**Purpose:** Lead with parental mental load rather than fear.

**Format:** 25–30 sec, 9:16. Parent-to-camera plus real installation B-roll.

**Script:**
> “Once my little one started exploring, I felt like I was saying ‘No, don’t touch that’ all day. Sharp furniture, open cabinets, sockets, the fridge and doors—there was always something else to manage. The Peach Bucket puts six childproofing categories into one organised kit. I can add protection around the areas they keep reaching, without buying everything separately. It’s ₹3,299. Tap to see exactly what comes inside.”

**On-screen reinforcement:**
- `For curious little explorers`
- `6 childproofing categories`
- `Designed around common Indian-home fixtures*`
- `₹3,299`
- `*Compatibility can vary; check before installation`

**Headline:** `Let them explore. Change the room.`

**Production note:** Use a genuine founder/team member or paid creator delivering an honest demonstration. Don’t present the script as a customer testimonial unless it reflects that person’s real experience.

## Launch plan

- Produce one master of each concept plus **two opening-hook variants**; keep the body identical so the hook is the main variable.
- Run them inside the purchase-optimised broad setup rather than creating “cheap click” campaigns.
- Give each concept enough budget/time to collect purchase signals; don’t pick a winner from CTR alone.
- Review: purchase CPA, purchase conversion value, landing-page-to-purchase rate and creative-level spend. Treat Meta checkouts and Shopify sessions as separate measurement systems.
- Your approximate pre-ad contribution is **₹2,233 per order** before RTO impact, taxes, packaging and reverse-shipping costs. Until those are confirmed, use ₹2,233 only as a provisional ceiling—not a scaling target.
- Do not use stock scarcity. Public page information was contradictory, and actual availability is unknown.",
